meta.description: Symptom -> cited-mechanism -> fix map for the diagnose fault-finder. Every fault references a mechanism slug in food-science-references.json so the explanation and citation come straight from the verified DB. Beverage-weighted for the professional beverage/mixology vertical.

faults.name: Cork taint (TCA)
faults.fix: Classic TCA: it mutes fruit and adds wet-cardboard/musty notes at parts-per-trillion. No rescue once it is in the bottle — reject the lot and trace the source (cork, wood, cellar air).

faults.name: Reductive off-aromas (volatile sulfur)
faults.fix: Volatile sulfur compounds from a too-reductive, low-oxygen environment. Often blows off with aeration/decanting; brief copper contact can scavenge it. Prevent with controlled oxygen and yeast nutrition.

faults.name: Oxidation (browning / aldehyde)
faults.fix: Oxidative browning plus acetaldehyde notes from too much oxygen and/or too little SO2, catalyzed by trace iron/copper. Not reversible — prevent with free-SO2 management and tighter closures.

faults.name: Diacetyl (buttery)
faults.fix: Diacetyl from malolactic/citrate metabolism — wanted in some Chardonnay, a fault in lager and most reds. Extend lees/MLF contact so bacteria reduce it to flavorless acetoin, or block MLF to avoid it entirely.

faults.name: Excess / harsh bitterness
faults.fix: Different bitters hit different receptors and do not simply add up. Rebalance with sweetness or a pinch of salt (both suppress bitter), cut the bittering agent, or swap to a softer bitter source rather than only diluting.

faults.name: Astringency (drying tannin)
faults.fix: Tannin-salivary-protein binding — a tactile drag, not a taste. Soften with body (sugar/glycerol), added protein/polysaccharide, or lower tannin and higher pH. Note sweetness will not mask it the way it masks bitter.

faults.name: Hot / boozy alcohol burn
faults.fix: Ethanol heat. A measured water/ice cut lowers ABV and pushes aroma to the surface ('opens up') — but do not over-dilute past roughly 20% added water, which flattens and homogenizes. Specify a target dilution.

faults.name: Aroma lost after dilution
faults.fix: Dropping ABV is not aroma-neutral — it dumps some volatiles to the headspace while muting others. Re-balance esters/aromatics for the served strength, or serve at the dilution where the nose actually peaks.

faults.name: Cloudy / hazy drink
faults.fix: Suspended proteins, polysaccharides, and polyphenols. Clarify by fining (milk-wash/casein, gelatin, agar), which also strips harsh tannins for a silkier texture. Match the agent to whatever is causing the haze.

faults.name: Flat head / no foam (beer)
faults.fix: Foam is a protein plus iso-alpha-acid film fighting lipids and ethanol. Raise foam-positive proteins/hop acids and eliminate fatty-acid/lipid carryover (grease on the glass is a frequent culprit). Strong beers need more support.

faults.name: Banana / clove off-character (beer)
faults.fix: Yeast esters (banana / isoamyl acetate) and phenols (clove / 4-vinylguaiacol). Style-defining in Hefeweizen, a fault in clean lagers — control with strain choice (POF+ vs POF-), fermentation temperature, and pitch rate.

faults.name: Over-extracted coffee (bitter/harsh)
faults.fix: Over-extraction: grind too fine, water too hot, or contact too long. Coarsen the grind, shorten contact, or lower temperature to land back in the ~18-22% yield window. Adjust grind before anything else.

faults.name: Under-extracted coffee (sour/weak)
faults.fix: Under-extraction: grind too coarse, water too cool, or flow too fast. Grind finer, raise temperature, or extend contact to reach the ~18-22% yield window. Sour-and-weak almost always means under-extracted.

faults.name: Over-oaked (too much vanilla/wood)
faults.fix: Lignin-derived vanillin / guaiacol / oak-lactone overload. Pull off the wood sooner, use older or less-toasted barrels (or fewer staves/chips), or blend back un-oaked base. Char depth and contact time are the dials.

faults.name: Weak / pale red color (wine)
faults.fix: Flavylium color is pH-driven. Target pH ~3.4-3.6 to maximize the red form, and add copigment cofactors (catechin, flavonols) to deepen and stabilize the hue — more color without more anthocyanin.

faults.name: Flat carbonation / no bite
faults.fix: The 'bite' is dissolved-CO2 acidity acting on trigeminal nerves, not just visible bubbles — so you cannot fake it with acid alone. Recarbonate cold, minimize headspace and agitation, and serve well chilled to hold CO2.

faults.name: Bitter / stewed tea (over-steeped)
faults.fix: Over-extraction of catechins. Shorten the steep, lower water temperature (especially for green/white), or use less leaf — pulling back astringency while keeping aroma and theanine sweetness.

faults.name: Greasy / oil-logged fried food
faults.fix: Most oil is absorbed during cooling as steam voids fill. Fry hot enough (160-180C) to build a fast crust, do not overcrowd (temperature crash), drain while hot, and replace tired/viscous oil — degraded oil fries greasier.

faults.name: Weeping / grainy meringue
faults.fix: The foam is a protein film at the air-water interface. Stabilize with a touch of acid (cream of tartar), zero fat contamination, and avoid over-whipping; weeping/beading usually means over-whipped or undissolved sugar.

faults.name: Grainy / gritty confection
faults.fix: Uncontrolled sucrose crystal growth. Cool undisturbed before beating, add a doctor (corn syrup/invertase) to interfere with crystals, and seed at the right temperature for many small, smooth crystals.

faults.name: Mushy / collapsed vegetables
faults.fix: Pectin beta-elimination in the middle lamella, fast above ~80C in low-acid water. Cook shorter and hotter, or use a low-temperature (50-60C) blanch plus calcium to firm the tissue before final cooking.

faults.name: Dull / olive-green vegetables
faults.fix: Acid plus heat swaps magnesium out of chlorophyll into olive pheophytin, irreversibly. Cook hot-and-fast, uncovered (to vent plant acids), and shock in ice water to lock the bright green.

faults.name: Brettanomyces / barnyard
faults.fix: Brettanomyces volatile phenols (4-ethylphenol/4-ethylguaiacol) above ~425 ug/L. A trace can add complexity; a lot suppresses fruit and reads barnyard/band-aid. Not cleanly removable — control by hygiene, SO2, and shorter/cooler oak aging.

faults.name: Volatile acidity (vinegar / nail polish)
faults.fix: Acetic acid + ethyl acetate from acetic-acid bacteria oxidizing ethanol under air. Above ~0.7 g/L it reads as spoilage; prevent with oxygen exclusion, topped-up vessels, and SO2 — it is not fixable after the fact.

faults.name: Hop creep (gushing / over-attenuation)
faults.fix: Hop amylolytic enzymes refermenting residual dextrins after dry-hopping — raises ABV and CO2 (a real bottle-bomb/safety risk) and can throw diacetyl. Rest/cold-crash or pasteurize before packaging, and budget for the extra attenuation.

faults.name: Stale / cardboard beer
faults.fix: Aldehyde staling (trans-2-nonenal and Strecker/Maillard aldehydes) from oxygen, heat, and malt heat load. Minimize package oxygen, store cold, and choose low-staling malt — not reversible once stale.

faults.name: Scorched / over-cooked agave spirit
faults.fix: Over-cooked agave drives furans/HMF and methanol with scorched notes; under-cooked loses fermentable sugar and body. The cook IS the flavor — control oven/autoclave time and temperature.

faults.name: Tartrate crystals ('wine diamonds')
faults.fix: Harmless potassium bitartrate from incomplete cold stabilization — a cosmetic/stability issue, not a taste fault. Cold-stabilize, or add CMC/mannoprotein/metatartaric acid to inhibit crystal growth before bottling.
